r.x: The Apple family

is the collective name for a group of classic shapes in the pipe repertoire that share a corner-free, rounded bowl. Apple sits at the family's core; Tomato, Egg, Acorn, and Brandy are all considered variations on the same soft silhouette, stretched and compressed in different proportions. What sets the family members apart, then, isn't ornamentation on the bowl but the ratio between its height and its width.
The Shared Form Logic

In the Apple family the bowl swells slightly toward the rim and narrows again as it approaches the base. There's no flat edge or sharp transition, and the join between bowl and shank is usually kept rounded as well. This geometry, unlike cylindrical-bowled shapes such as Billiard, leaves a spherical gripping surface in the hand. The fact that the bowl wall can stay relatively thick is also one of the reasons the family is chosen so often; in general shape classifications, the Apple family is accordingly discussed under the "round group" heading. For detailed terminology, see the pipe anatomy entry.
The family is made in both straight and bent bodies. In bent versions, the continuity the bowl forms with the curved shank is often preferred because it emphasizes the family's soft line.
Members of the Family
Apple:
The standard itself. The bowl sits close to a sphere resembling an apple, with height and width close to each other.
Tomato:

A flattened version of Apple. The bowl lowers while widening at the sides. It can be confused with a separately named shape found in some sources, Ball; Ball is regarded as nearly fully spherical, while Tomato is noticeably squat.
Egg:
Apple stretched along the vertical axis. The elliptical bowl is most often paired with a curved shank, giving the family's longest profile.
Acorn:
Named after the acorn. The bowl reaches its widest point in its upper half and tapers quickly as it descends; in many examples this narrowing leaves a slim tip below the bowl-shank joint.
Brandy:
Named after the brandy snifter. A bowl that flares from a wide base toward the rim, the family's most goblet-like member.

These distinctions aren't drawn with hard lines. The same pipe can be called Apple in one catalog and Tomato in another; this drift of shape names across manufacturer catalogs is a general problem detailed in the classification of pipe shapes entry.
Historical Background

Round-bowled shapes have been known since the clay pipe era; but the naming as it exists today became settled with the institutionalization of the briar industry in the mid-19th century. According to records, briar pipe production in the French town of Saint-Claude began in the mid-1850s, and by 1860 the country's factory count had reached ten. The hardness and heat resistance of the material made thick-walled round bowls — difficult in clay — feasible for mass production, and Apple became part of the core repertoire that settled in during this period. Exactly when the shape names took on their present meanings can't be traced with certainty from the catalogs. One reason the family remains popular today is its suitability for turning; another is that it offers a foundation open to free interpretation in handmade production.

r.x: Çubuk
(known in Western languages as the
chibouk
or
tchibouque

) is the traditional long-stemmed pipe of the Ottoman world, whose length could exceed a meter and reach as much as a meter and a half. The origin of its name is debated: some sources trace the word to the Persian
çûbek
(little stick), while some etymological dictionaries link it to the Old Turkic root
çıbık

(thin branch); in either case, the word passed from Turkish into the Balkan languages and into Western languages. After tobacco's arrival on Ottoman soil, the chibouk spread widely in the 17th century and remained part of daily life for more than two centuries across a broad geography stretching from the Balkans to Iran. This entry treats the chibouk as an object; the hospitality and social customs that grew up around it are described in the entry on chibouk culture in the Ottoman Empire.
Structure and Parts
Unlike modern pipes carved from a single block, the chibouk is formed from the union of three separate parts:
Bowl (lüle):
A fired clay chamber that holds the tobacco. It fits onto the end of the stem and can be replaced on its own when worn out or broken.
Stem (çubuk):
The long shaft that gives the pipe its name, made from jasmine, cherry, or rosewood. The smoke cools as it travels through this long channel.
Mouthpiece (imame):
The part that meets the lips; usually made of amber.

This three-part arrangement is essentially the Ottoman equivalent of the bowl-shank-mouthpiece layout of today's pipe anatomy; it is thanks to the chibouk that the words "lüle" and "imame" still survive in Turkish pipe terminology today. On fine examples, the amber mouthpiece was known to be set with precious stones and the stem wrapped in silver wire; the length and ornamentation of a chibouk were considered a mark of its owner's social standing.
The Bowl and Tophane Craftsmanship

The chibouk's most characteristic part, the clay bowl, was shaped from red clay using a mold and then finished by hand. In this respect it differs from Europe's single-piece white clay pipes both in color and in being designed as a component independent of the shank. The center of bowl production was the Tophane district of Istanbul; gilded, silver-inlaid Tophane bowls are regarded as one of the signature products of Ottoman handicraft, and today they are catalogued in museum collections and auction listings under the name "Ottoman chibouk with Tophane bowl."
Relationship to Western Pipes and Decline

A formal parallel is often drawn between the chibouk and Europe's long-stemmed Churchwarden tradition; some sources note that this long-stemmed design spread in Europe under Eastern influence from the 17th century onward, though the direction and extent of that influence are not conclusively documented. What structurally sets the chibouk apart from its relatives is that the bowl is a separate clay piece that can be removed and replaced, meaning the same stem could be used with dozens of different bowls over the decades.

With the rise of cigarettes and the water pipe toward the end of the century, use of the chibouk declined rapidly, and Tophane bowl-making itself died out at the beginning of the 20th century. Today the chibouk survives less as a functional pipe than as a historical craft object; through the words it contributed to Turkish pipe terminology, it forms a bridge between the modern pipe and Ottoman tradition.

r.x: The Canadian family

is a four-member shape group bringing together the long-shanked derivatives of the classic Billiard: Canadian, Lumberman, Liverpool, and Lovat. In all four, the bowl keeps Billiard proportions; what truly defines the family is a shank kept considerably longer than usual, paired with a short stem. The long shank places more absorbent briar between the burning tobacco and the smoker's lips, letting the smoke cool and shed moisture along the way; the family is known for this cool, dry smoke.
The Matrix That Separates the Four Members

The family's members are distinguished by the answers to two simple questions: Is the shank's cross-section oval or round? Is the stem tapered or saddle? These two questions, each with two possible answers, form a 2x2 matrix that yields the family's four members:

By this logic, Liverpool is considered the member closest in silhouette to the Canadian, while Lovat sits at the opposite corner of the matrix from the Canadian. All four members are held to share the same smoking character; the difference among them lies in the shape of the shank and stem rather than in the smoke itself. These definitions reflect a broad consensus in the community, but not every maker follows the matrix to the letter, and the boundaries can blur in some catalogues. The definitions are therefore best read as common convention rather than a strict standard. All four variants have appeared over the years in the catalogues of established makers such as Peterson and Comoy's of London.
Proportion and the Challenge of Making One

The family's shared aesthetic rule is proportion: the shank is typically 1.5 to 2 times the height of the bowl, while the stem is kept correspondingly short. Keeping the stem short is not unique to the Canadian — it's a rule common to all four members. When this balance is thrown off and the stem lengthens, the shape is considered to lose its character and become nothing more than an ordinary "long Billiard."

Making a true Canadian is considered a demanding piece of craft, since the long shank is expected to come out of the same block of briar as the bowl, in one piece. That calls for a large, flawless block; because such blocks are scarce, well-made Canadians hold a special place among collectors. For the naming of parts like the bowl, shank, and stem, see pipe anatomy.
Origins of the Names

The origins of the names within the family are largely uncertain. Where the name "Canadian" comes from is unknown; the shape has no documented manufacturing link to Canada. The name "Lovat" is said to be connected to Simon Fraser, the Scottish lord who founded the Lovat Scouts, though this link is undocumented. The family is classified among the Billiard derivatives, on the straight side of the classic pipe shapes catalogue.

r.x: Pipe anatomy

covers the parts of a pipe and the names given to them. Though seemingly a simple object, a pipe is made up of two main parts: the body (stummel), which contains the tobacco chamber and shank, and the mouthpiece (stem), taken into the mouth. Knowing these terms makes it easier to understand shape names and to follow discussions of care and smoking technique.
The Body: Bowl, Chamber and Shank

The body's most visible part is the bowl: the outer shell that surrounds the tobacco chamber, held in the hand while the pipe is filled and smoked. On most of today's pipes, the bowl is carved from briar. The cavity inside the bowl is called the chamber; tobacco is packed and lit here, and the chamber's diameter and depth directly affect the smoking character. The top surface of the bowl is called the rim, and its lowest point the heel. The heel matters both for cleaning and for the even development over time of the protective layer of carbon (cake) that builds up through smoking.

The section connecting the bowl to the mouthpiece is the shank. Running through the inside of the shank, from the base of the chamber to the end of the mouthpiece, is the smoke channel (draft hole). How straight and centered this channel is drilled is considered one of the primary measures of a pipe's craftsmanship.
Mouthpiece and Connection System

The mouthpiece (stem) is the part connecting the shank to the bite section; today it's most often made of ebonite (vulcanite) or acrylic. For a comparison of materials, see the mouthpiece materials entry. The fitting system that connects the mouthpiece to the body is called the mortise-tenon: the socket in the shank is the mortise, and the cylindrical projection at the end of the mouthpiece is the tenon. This fit provides an airtight but removable connection. In some pipes a 9mm activated-carbon or balsa filter is placed in the mortise, and in some models a metal piece called a "stinger," intended to reduce moisture and harshness, is fitted; details are in the pipe filters and systems entry.

The final section of the mouthpiece taken into the mouth (roughly its last 2.5 centimeters) is the bit. Some sources use "stem" and "bit" interchangeably; in this encyclopedia, mouthpiece refers to the whole part, and bit refers only to its tip. The raised projection at the tip is called the button; the pipe rests behind the teeth on this projection and is held without slipping. The flat opening where smoke exits toward the mouth is the slot, the final point of the smoke channel. In terms of form, mouthpieces fall into two main groups: tapered, which narrows to a point, and saddle, which is stepped.

r.x: Proportions and Multi-Piece Traditions

Just as important as the names of the parts is the ratio between them. On a classic Billiard pipe, for example, the shank length is expected to roughly equal the bowl height, and the mouthpiece to be 1.4-1.5 times the shank. Such ratios are taken as a mark of craftsmanship when defining classic pipe shapes. On the other hand, today's arrangement — body and mouthpiece joined by a single connection — is relatively recent: in examples like the German-Tyrolean tradition's fitted pipes (Gesteckpfeife) and the Ottoman çubuk, a pipe is a multi-piece object, and today's briar pipe is understood to have spread in the mid-19th century in the wake of these traditions.

r.x: Bulldog and Rhodesian

are a pair, instantly recognizable, among the classic pipe shapes. Both have a body that resembles two cones set base to base, with the body's widest point most often encircled by one or two beadlines. What separates the two shapes has been debated for as long as anyone can remember; for that reason they're usually treated together, under a single heading, in comparison.
Double-Cone Body and Beadlines

What gives the shape its character is the geometry of the bowl: the lower section forms a cone widening upward, the upper section a cone narrowing toward the rim. The line where the two cones meet, the widest point, is emphasized by beadlines running around it. These lines aren't purely decorative — they mark the join of the two cones. Since these lines are generally cut on the lathe, working them clean and symmetrical, especially on a handmade pipe, is taken as a sign of skill. Against the calm cylinder of the Billiard shape, the double-cone body offers a sharp-lined, almost architectural look. For the naming of body sections, see the pipe anatomy entry.
Which Is Bulldog, Which Is Rhodesian?
The most common modern consensus is based on the cross-section of the shank:

A Bulldog is typically made with a slightly forward-leaning bowl and a diamond-sectioned saddle mouthpiece. In some definitions, though, it's the body's stance rather than the cross-section that's taken as the criterion, with the bent version counted as Rhodesian. Either way, one point matters: the rule "diamond shank is Bulldog, round shank is Rhodesian" is a customary consensus, not a historical standard. Because pipe shape names were never formally standardized in any period, some manufacturers in the past called both forms "Bulldog," others "Rhodesian," and the debate continues in the pipe community today.
Origin and Naming

The shape emerged in English pipe production in the late 19th century. The name "Rhodesian" is thought to refer to Rhodesia, then a British colony (today's Zimbabwe and Zambia); but exactly when and by whom the name was first used has never been documented. The vogue for naming shapes after southern Africa in that period also carries over into the Oom Paul shape from the same era. By the early 20th century, both forms had entered the catalog classics of English brands such as Dunhill, Comoy's of London, and GBD; the fact that Bulldog codes formed a separate group in Dunhill's old shape numbering system shows how much weight the shape carried in catalog tradition.

Today the double-cone body is considered a classic that nearly every factory and craftsman puts their own stamp on: countless straight, bent, long-shank, and squat variations are made. Whatever name it goes by, the beaded double-cone silhouette remains one of the most enduring signatures in pipe design.

r.x: Poker and Cherrywood

are two shapes that grow out of a shared structural idea: the bottom of the bowl is flattened, so the pipe stands on a table or stand without any support. Any pipe with this feature is broadly known among enthusiasts as a "sitter" pipe; Poker and Cherrywood are the best-known, most standardized members of that family.
Poker

The Poker is an upright shape in which a near-cylindrical bowl meets a straight shank. The bowl walls are usually kept thick, the base is wide and flat, and the transition where the shank meets the bowl is slightly raised in most examples. Viewed from the side, this profile is most often compared in shape guides to a mallet; the comparison is descriptive rather than exact. Measured against a billiard of the same size, it gives a heavier, more massive impression — part of the bowl's volume goes toward the thick material that spreads the heat.

The shape's practical rationale is clear. At a writing desk, while reading, or with your hands full, the pipe can be set down without needing a separate stand. Because the shank is short, the mouthpiece is easy to grip, and the pipe's center of gravity stays close to its base.
Cherrywood

The Cherrywood is the curved-shank relative of that same flat-bottomed bowl. The short description is the same across every guide: a Poker with its shank and mouthpiece bent. The shank rises from the bowl at an angle or in a gentle curve, and the mouthpiece is usually bent. This keeps the pipe's sitting ability while giving it a balance better suited to being carried clenched in the teeth.

The name is generally taken to come from the material the earliest examples were made of; this explanation is common in guide sources, though it hasn't been traced to a primary document. Records show that the French maker Eugène-Léon Ropp patented a pipe made from wild cherry wood in 1869, and the following year he set up a workshop to produce them at Bussang, in the Vosges mountains. These pipes became the brand's long-running mainstay, and over time the shape itself became detached from the material, turning into a shape name applied to pipes in any material, briar chief among them. Today, the word "cherrywood" in a catalogue mostly describes this silhouette rather than the type of wood.
Distinction and Relatives

The one deciding factor that separates the two shapes is the curve of the shank and mouthpiece: straight counts as a Poker, curved as a Cherrywood. The flat base is common to both and isn't distinctive on its own, since flattening the heel can be applied to other shapes as well. That's why, in shape classification, the sitter pipe is treated not as a family but as a trait.

As the bowl's outline moves away from a cylinder, the naming changes too: conical or barrel-shaped bowls take their own names, and examples with entirely free-form proportions shift into the territory of the freehand. Among classic shape lists, Poker and Cherrywood, thanks to their simple geometry, are two patterns turned to often both in mass production and in hand-shaping.

r.x: Lumberman

is a straight pipe shape formed by joining a long, oval-sectioned shank (shank) with a short saddle mouthpiece (saddle stem). It's part of the four-member group known as the Canadian family; like the other members, it inherits its bowl proportions from the classic Billiard shape, differing only in the form of its shank and mouthpiece. It's regarded in the community as one of the family's rarest combinations.
Two Criteria That Define the Shape

The four members of the Canadian family diverge at the intersection of two simple criteria: whether the shank cross-section is oval or round, and whether the mouthpiece is tapered or saddle-type. Lumberman falls into the "oval shank + saddle mouthpiece" cell of this chart. Canadian, which uses the same oval shank cross-section with a tapered mouthpiece, is Lumberman's closest relative; when the two shapes are set side by side, the only difference is whether the mouthpiece has a shoulder or tapers continuously end to end. When that same saddle mouthpiece is paired with a round-sectioned shank instead, the shape is called Lovat.

The commonly cited criterion for shank length is that the shank exceeds twice the bowl height. The short saddle mouthpiece balances the pipe against this long shank; if the proportion is thrown off by lengthening the mouthpiece, the shape is considered to lose its character. For the naming of parts such as shank, bowl, and mouthpiece, see the pipe anatomy entry.
Smoking Character and Construction

A shared trait of long-shanked shapes is that they put more briar between the burning tobacco and the lip. Because smoke gets the chance to cool and shed moisture over that distance, Lumberman, like the rest of the family, is known for a cool, dry smoke. In this respect no significant difference in smoking character is drawn out within the family; the distinction lies largely in silhouette and hand-feel.

On the production side, because the long shank needs to be cut from the same block as the body in one piece, it calls for a large, flawless block. Smoothly joining the saddle mouthpiece's shoulder to the oval shank also requires separate craftsmanship; the smallest misalignment at the shank-mouthpiece join stands out faster on an oval cross-section than it would on a round one. These two difficulties together are used to explain why the shape appears so rarely in mass-production catalogs.
Catalog History and Naming

This four-member classification has become established largely through Bill Burney's widely circulated shape charts. Manufacturers, though, don't follow the chart to the letter. For example, in Peterson records, Lumberman is defined among the long-shanked shapes but doesn't appear as a model listed under its own name in catalog pages; pipes of similar dimensions have most often appeared under the Canadian or Lovat heading. This is why name and dimension often conflict in the classification of old pipes; classification is done based more on shank cross-section and mouthpiece type than on the stamped name.

The name's origin is undocumented. There's no solid record of how the word — meaning "woodcutter" — came to be attached to the shape; the origins of the family's Canadian and Lovat names are similarly unclear. The shape is evaluated on the straight wing of the classic pipe shapes lineup, among the Billiard derivatives.

r.x: Lovat

is a classic pipe shape formed by the union of a long, round-shanked neck with a short saddle stem. It belongs to the four-member group known as the Canadian family, and within that group it is considered the member whose silhouette sits furthest from the Canadian itself. Like the whole family, the bowl keeps Billiard proportions; what actually defines the shape is not the bowl but the ratio between the shank and the mouthpiece.
Distinguishing Lines

The four members of the Canadian family are distinguished by two criteria: the shank's cross-section and the type of mouthpiece. The Lovat is the member that pairs a round shank with a saddle stem. The Canadian, with its oval shank and tapered stem, and the Liverpool, with its round shank but tapered stem, both differ from the Lovat on this point; the Lumberman shares the saddle stem but has an oval shank. A saddle stem is one that forms a thick shoulder where it meets the shank and then tapers into a flat, straight tongue; kept short, it gives the pipe a compact, almost clipped look. For the naming of these parts, see the entry on pipe anatomy.

Compared with the rest of the family, the Lovat's shank is generally more restrained. Some classification attempts give a guideline that the shank length shouldn't exceed twice the bowl's height; this isn't a standard everyone follows, just an approximation used to describe the shape. That's why, even though the Lovat is grouped under long-shanked pipes, it's regarded as the most compact-silhouetted member of the group. As the shank lengthens, the smoke touches more briar surface before it reaches the mouth; the shape's reputation among enthusiasts for a cool, dry smoke rests on this observation.
Name and History

The shape's name is tied to the title of Lovat used in Scottish nobility, though sources disagree on which Lord Lovat it's attributed to. At least three different names circulate in pipe literature: some sources point to the 14th Lord Lovat, Simon Joseph Fraser; others cite a different Fraser with different life dates; still others mention an entirely different Lovat Fraser. Since the names and dates don't agree with one another, this connection should be read as an established narrative rather than a documented fact.

The shape's catalogue history is on firmer ground. According to accounts, one of the first makers to use this name in this form was the English firm BBB; the Lovat is recorded as having appeared in BBB catalogues in four separate sizes before the First World War. Over the course of the twentieth century, the shape became a fixture in English and Irish makers' catalogues. In Dunhill's numbering system, the code denoting a Lovat is 111; in the Shell Briar line's 41111 stamp, for example, the leading 4 indicates the size group, the second digit marks the saddle stem, and the trailing 111 denotes the shape itself. It remains a regular presence today in the catalogues of both established mass-production brands and individual makers working alone.

r.x: Classic pipe shapes

is the collective name for body forms established over generations in pipe making, whose names and proportions have been passed down by tradition. These names have never been tied to a formal standard; the same shape can appear under different names in two manufacturers' catalogs. Even so, there's consensus around a core repertoire, and its archetype is taken to be Billiard: shapes like Pot, Apple, and Panel are defined as its many derivatives.
Straight, Bent, and Free Form

Shapes are classified along two major axes. The first is the body's stance: straight and bent. Bending isn't a shape in itself but a qualifier; "Bent Billiard" or "Bent Apple" means the same body, bent. Degree of bend is referred to as 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and full bent. The second axis lies between classic molds and free form: classic shapes stick to certain proportions and lines, while freehand pipes step outside those molds.

r.x: The boundaries aren't always sharp: the line between Apple and Tomato, or Acorn and Dublin, can shift from one manufacturer to another. The name Poker is said to have arisen from the need to set the pipe down at the card table; the origins of names like Zulu and Cutty rest largely on oral tradition.
How Shape Affects the Smoke

Shape isn't purely an aesthetic choice; bowl geometry directly affects the smoking experience. In the conical Dublin, flavor intensifies as the tobacco diminishes toward the base; wide-mouthed shapes like Pot and Prince burn more tobacco surface at once and so bring aroma to the fore. Because the full-bent body shifts the center of gravity toward the jaw, Oom Paul is considered the large-volume shape best suited to clenching. Flat-based types like Poker, meanwhile, are known as pipes often set down and picked back up at the table.
Factory Shape Numbers

Major factories such as Dunhill, Comoy's, GBD, and Peterson identified shapes throughout the 20th century by catalog number rather than by name. Dunhill's own system had roughly fifty separate codes just for the Billiard; the LB code is understood to mean "Large Billiard." At Peterson, numbers like 999 (Rhodesian) and 02 (Oom Paul) have become synonymous with the shape's identity. These numbers don't translate between brands: the same number can denote entirely different shapes in two brands. Archived shape charts are, today, the basic tool used for dating estate pipes.

r.x: Churchwarden

is a pipe type whose bowl can take almost any classic form, but whose mouthpiece (stem) is kept unusually long. The mouthpiece alone can reach 22-45 cm; total length most often falls between 25 and 40 cm. Because the long stem lets smoke cool over the entire distance before it reaches the mouth, the shape is known for a cool smoke. Within classic pipe shapes, Churchwarden is one of the rare types defined by proportions rather than bowl shape.
Shape and Smoking Traits

What defines the Churchwarden is length: the bowl can take any classic form — billiard, apple, Dublin, and so on — and the mouthpiece can be either straight or curved. Besides a cool smoke, the long stem also keeps the bowl away from the face, so its heat and smoke don't bother the eyes. This is also why German-speaking countries call similar long pipes "Lesepfeife" (reading pipe): smoke doesn't drift into the field of view of a reader bent over a book. On the other hand, the long stem shifts the balance forward; the pipe isn't suited to clenching between the teeth and needs to be held in the hand throughout a smoke. Cleaning also requires pipe cleaners longer than standard.
History

The shape's roots can be traced on two layers. The long-stemmed pipe tradition goes back to the clay pipes that spread across Europe from the 17th century onward; the long-stemmed clay pipes known as "aldermen" are said to have been shared, communal items in taverns, belonging to the establishment and passing from one customer to the next. Its formation into today's shape under the name "Churchwarden" dates to a later period, the late 18th to early 19th century. Records indicate that Eastern influence also played a role in the spread of the long-stemmed design in Europe; in this respect the shape bears a striking parallel to the Ottoman çubuk. With the spread of briar in the mid-1800s, the Churchwarden moved from clay to wood and took its place in classic pipe catalogs.
Origin of the Name
Where the name comes from hasn't been documented; a few explanations circulate together in the community:
Officials who kept watch over churches at night (churchwardens) are said to have preferred this long pipe on duty because it didn't block their view.
Another account has church officials smoking it by hanging it out a window.
It's also suggested that the shape was named by comparison to long-handled candle snuffers.
None of these explanations is considered superior to the others; the name is accepted as having grown out of these kinds of associations with the figure of the church official in England.
Churchwarden Today
Gandalf and the hobbits smoking Churchwardens in Peter Jackson's
The Lord of the Rings

film trilogy (2001-2003) brought the shape a strong wave of popularity in the 21st century. Among the best-known mass-produced examples is the Churchwarden series from the Peterson brand; some German and Italian manufacturers also include this type in their catalogs. With its long stem and its evocation of a fantasy world, the Churchwarden is regarded as a shape synonymous with unhurried, long, quiet sessions.

r.x: Liverpool

is a straight pipe shape formed by joining a long, round-sectioned shank with a short, tapered mouthpiece (stem). The bowl proportions preserve Billiard dimensions; what actually defines the shape is the unusually long distance the shank runs from bowl to lip. Because of this, Liverpool is classified as part of the four-member group known as the Canadian family.
Its Place in the Family

The members of the Canadian family are distinguished by two variables: the shank's cross-section and the mouthpiece type. Liverpool falls into the box where a round shank meets a tapered mouthpiece in this grid. Canadian also uses a tapered mouthpiece, but its shank is oval-sectioned; the only thing separating the two shapes, then, is the shank's cross-section, and from a distance their silhouettes look almost identical. Lovat shares the same round shank as Liverpool but is finished with a saddle-type mouthpiece. These definitions are largely credited to Bill Burney's widely used shape charts, which group all four shapes together under the heading "long shanks." For a detailed comparison, see the long shanks entry.

On proportion, the criterion often cited in the community is that on a Liverpool the shank length exceeds twice the bowl height. The same criterion is generally kept more modest for Lovat; a Lovat's shank most often stays below that limit. Since the boundaries shift from one manufacturer to another, these definitions should be understood as an established convention rather than a strict standard.
Construction and Smoke

The long shank is expected to be cut in one piece with the bowl, from the same briar block. Because this requires a block that's both large and flawless, Liverpool is among the shapes rarely seen in mass production. The long shank is also functional: because more absorbent wood sits between the burning tobacco and the lip, the smoke is thought to cool and shed moisture along the way. The family's members share this smoking character; where they differ is in shape. For the naming of parts like shank, bowl, and mouthpiece, see the pipe anatomy entry.
Its Trail in the Catalogs

Where the shape's name comes from hasn't been documented; the link drawn to the English city of Liverpool is an assumption unsupported by records. The shape's catalog history, though, can be traced. In Dunhill's shape lists, tapered-mouthpiece Liverpool counterparts appear under numbers 33, 36, and 331. According to compilations, 33 corresponds to the standard-sized Liverpool, 36 to its larger sibling, and 331 to the long-shanked version; all three numbers are recorded as appearing in catalogs stretching from the late 1920s to the late 1960s. This means the shape stayed in the brand's lineup for roughly half a century. Peterson, meanwhile, referred to the same shape in its own traditional terminology as "Bolton"; this naming appears in the records of researchers who have studied the brand, but exactly which years the usage spanned hasn't been clearly documented.

r.x: The classification of pipe shapes

is the name for the effort to bring order to the confusion caused by different manufacturers calling the same form by different names. Shape names in pipe making have never, in any period, been tied to a standards body; names have become established by passing from workshop to workshop, catalog to catalog. For this reason, three separate levels are used together when describing a pipe: the traditional name, the body's stance, and the manufacturer's own number. The classic pipe shapes entry gives the repertoire of these names, while this entry addresses the system itself.
Family Logic

Shapes are thought of not individually but in rings of kinship. By common consensus the starting point is Billiard: forms like Lovat, Liverpool, Canadian, Lumberman, Pot, Panel, Apple, and Dublin are considered derivatives of the same basic body, obtained by altering proportion, shank length, and mouthpiece (stem) arrangement. Describing a shape therefore takes more than memorizing its name; measurable traits such as the degree of the bowl's (bowl) taper, wall thickness, shank cross-section, and heel shape are what actually distinguish it. The terms in the pipe anatomy entry are the shared language for these measurements.

The second axis is stance. The straight and bent distinction isn't a shape in itself but a qualifier placed in front of an existing shape; Bent Billiard and Billiard are two states of the same family. Bodies that step entirely outside classic molds, meanwhile, are gathered under the freehand heading and are referred to not by shape name but by their designer's signature.
Factory Numbers

From the late 19th century onward, the major factories tried to overcome the ambiguity of names with numbers. According to records, Comoy's both named and numbered its shapes in its 1909 catalog; but stamping these numbers onto the pipes themselves only became widespread in the 1920s, and the earliest known stamped example is dated to 1925. Comoy's numbers stayed three digits for a long time; after the brand passed into the Cadogan group in 1979, four-digit codes also began to appear.

Dunhill turned a single number into a multi-layered code. In the brand's matured system, the first digit of the code indicates the bowl size group, the second the mouthpiece form, and the remaining digits the shape itself; for example, 4103 corresponds to a tapered-mouthpiece Billiard from the fourth group. The group scale, numbered one through six, is recorded as having come into use in 1954, and roughly corresponds to chamber volume, though it isn't a precise measure since it varies from shape to shape. The group number being folded into the code as the first digit of the shape number happened later, said to be in the second half of the 1970s; before that, the group was printed as a separate stamp. Charatan's own one-through-six scale carries a similar logic; it's known that the same number doesn't denote the same size across two brands.
Limits of the System

These codes are consistent within a brand but untranslatable between brands: a number's meaning can only be resolved with the chart printed by the manufacturer that used it. Archived shape charts are, for this reason, considered a basic tool for identifying and dating estate pipes. On the naming side, the documentary basis is much weaker; the story behind many shape names has been carried forward by oral tradition, and this debate is addressed separately in the origin of briar pipe shape names entry.

r.x: Cavalier

is a pipe shape whose shank extends downward beneath the bowl, carrying a removable cap at the end of this extension. In an ordinary pipe the shank runs in a single direction, back from the bowl; on a Cavalier, though, the shank doesn't just stay behind the bowl — it descends, giving the pipe a kind of foot. Thanks to this foot, the pipe can stand upright on a table without tipping over. The shape isn't common today; it turns up mostly in one-off artisan work and in old catalogs.
Structure and Working Principle

What defines the Cavalier is less its look than its drilling layout. Two separate holes run through the shank: the first passes the full length of the shank end to end, the second connects the bottom of the bowl to that main channel. As smoke passes from the bottom of the bowl into the shank, moisture condensing out of it drops by gravity to the lowest point of the shank — the capped extension — and collects there. That way, moisture doesn't collect in the smoke channel or the mouthpiece, the most sensitive spot in terms of pipe anatomy.

The cap at the end of the extension can be threaded or push-fit. When removed, it lets accumulated liquid be emptied and also lets a cleaner be passed straight through the pipe via a direct channel. In this respect the Cavalier is counted among the solutions that push the job of managing moisture onto the body's design; for other mechanisms tackling the same problem from a different angle, see pipe filters and systems.
Origin
The shape's origin is traced to Central Europe's tradition of pipes built from separate pieces. The German word
Gesteckpfeife

means, literally, "pipe assembled from parts": the bowl, chamber, shank, and mouthpiece were each made separately and then fitted together. Common in German and Austrian culture from the 18th century into the early 20th, these pipes are also known as the Tyrolean pipe, associated with the Tyrol region. The bowl was most often porcelain; the chamber beneath it caught the tobacco's moisture and tar, and wine was sometimes added inside it for flavor.

According to commercial shape guides, from the late 19th century onward this arrangement was adapted to the briar pipe and began to be known in English production as the Cavalier; it can't be said that the connection has been examined in any academic study. The name Cavalier appears in Dunhill's shape lists, and surviving interwar examples are recorded as "Tyrolean cavalier"; other English manufacturers such as Comoy's are also said to have made similar pipes. Exactly where the shape's name comes from hasn't been conclusively documented.
Its Standing Today

The Cavalier rarely appears in standard shape lists; for that reason it most often shows up in the classification of pipe shapes not as an independent family but as a subheading defined by its shank extension. Bowl shape is unconstrained: billiard, apple, or freer bodies can all be adapted to the Cavalier arrangement; the shank can be straight or bent. This flexibility makes the shape appealing for artisan production, because what really matters isn't the bowl's silhouette but the shank's downward-reaching arm and its cap.

In practice, the two-hole layout demands a more careful axis calculation than an ordinary pipe requires; when the point where the channels meet drifts off, both draw and cleaning suffer. This construction difficulty is also thought to have played a part in why the shape never became widespread.

r.x: Dublin

is a classic pipe shape known for its conical bowl, which widens toward the top and narrows toward the base. It carries a shank and mouthpiece of the same general proportions as the cylindrical-bowled Billiard; the only thing that sets them apart is the bowl geometry. It's recorded as one of the oldest bowl shapes inherited from the pre-briar clay pipe tradition, which is why it's most often listed right alongside the Billiard in shape guides.
Origin of the Name

The shape's name may look like it comes straight from Ireland's capital, but how this connection was ever made isn't known; shape guides agree that no satisfying explanation for the name's origin exists. One frequently offered guess links the word to the Irish
dúidín
Dúidín
is a diminutive of
dúd

, meaning "pipe," and describes a short clay pipe; but this resemblance is just a similarity of words — there's no record showing the naming actually comes from there. A second guess is that the name doesn't refer to a particular production center but reflects the traditional naming habits of 19th-century catalogs. As with most shape names, there's no single proven explanation here either; this uncertainty is part of the general problem discussed in the classification of pipe shapes entry.
Shape and Use

The inner surface of the Dublin's bowl also opens conically, mirroring the outside — meaning the combustion chamber is narrow at the base and wide at the rim. The practical result of this "V" cross-section is that a narrower burning area is left at the bottom of the tobacco. It's a common belief in the community that the conical chamber intensifies the burn toward the end and reduces the need for relights; this is a shared user impression, not a measured finding.

Because wall thickness increases around the base, Dublin bowls can stay relatively light, which makes the shape well suited to thin shanks and balanced designs. The rim is most often cut flat, though it can be inward-sloped or rounded depending on the maker. For the shape's components, see the pipe anatomy entry.
Variations
The Dublin family expands as bowl angle and shank shape are altered:
Zulu:
A variation in which the Dublin bowl is tilted noticeably forward, paired with a slightly curved mouthpiece. It also appears in sources under the names
Woodstock
and
Yachtsman
; it's considered a rarely seen shape in catalogs.
Cutty:
A form that directly preserves the clay-pipe silhouette with a thin, long, forward-leaning bowl.
Acorn:
A shape that softens the conical bowl with rounded lines, often confused with the Dublin.
Bent Dublin:
A rarer catalog variant that pairs the same bowl with a curved shank and mouthpiece.

In Irish production, the shape appears from early on. According to sources compiling the brand's history, straight, cone-bowled models were already present in Peterson's first catalog in 1896; the name "Dublin" wasn't yet used on these early pages, where shapes were identified only by number. The name became established in later catalogs, and the shape has been carried forward with new numbers across different periods of the brand's history. It remains among the standard shapes in both factory and workshop production today; for a detailed comparison, see the classic pipe shapes entry.

r.x: Billiard

is the straight shape considered the most classic of all pipe shapes; it's found in nearly every manufacturer's catalog, and other shapes are often described in relation to it. With its near-cylindrical bowl, measured shank length, and unassuming line, it sits at the center of the classic pipe shapes family. Unless otherwise qualified, a Billiard is a straight pipe; when its mouthpiece is bent, it's called a "Bent Billiard."
Shape and Proportions

The Billiard's bowl is nearly cylindrical; its base is rounded, and the bowl leans slightly outward and back from the shank by a few degrees. This small tilt gives the shape a lively stance rather than the look of a rigid mold standing bolt upright. For the names of parts such as bowl, shank, and mouthpiece, see the pipe anatomy entry.
The shape's classic proportions are summarized as follows:
Bowl height is roughly 1.25 times the bowl diameter.
Shank length is close to the bowl height.
The pipe's total length is a little more than three times the bowl height.
These figures aren't rigid rules but balance measurements refined through makers' trained eye; small deviations from one manufacturer to another are considered normal.

On a Billiard that keeps faithfully to the classic description, the chamber is also cylindrical; because the outer surface and the inner bore rise on the same axis, the rim comes out as a flat ring of even thickness all the way around. Leaving a very slight bulge in the middle of the wall is a common practice; this adds a bit of extra wood thickness at the point where heat concentrates most. Examples with a rounded rim or one narrowing upward are also made; although these are considered departures from the standard, as long as the body doesn't drift toward an apple or egg look, it's still counted as a Billiard. The shank cross-section is classically round, and the mouthpiece is most often of the tapered type.
Shank, Mouthpiece and Bend Variations

The same body turns into a whole set of subtypes as the shank cross-section and mouthpiece shape change. When a saddle mouthpiece is fitted instead of a tapered one, the pipe takes the name "Saddle Billiard." The shank can be worked round, oval, diamond-sectioned, or in a thin "pencil" form instead of round. When the surfaces of the body or shank are flattened, a Panel Billiard is born; when a box-shaped bowl meets a square shank, the result is a type called "Four-Square." An army mount, where the shank is wrapped in a metal band and the mouthpiece is push-fitted, is also a solution often paired with the Billiard body.

In old catalogs, degree of bend was indicated with fractions: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and full bent. This scale has no precise measured equivalent; the line between 3/4 and full bent especially remains approximate in practice. For a Billiard bent all the way, with a shank rising nearly vertically, the names Oom Paul or Hungarian are used. The name Oom Paul is traced to Paul Kruger, president of the South African Republic in the late 19th century.
Origin and Naming

The Billiard is thought to have matured in the 19th century, as mass production of pipes from briar on the lathe developed. This maturation is mostly associated with England; but the share of the Saint-Claude workshops in France in this process is also a matter of debate. It's suggested that the name comes from the flat, plain form of a billiard cue; but this explanation of its origin isn't conclusively documented.
The Billiard Family
The Billiard is such a fundamental shape that a substantial part of the classic repertoire is considered a derivative of it:

rows: Flattened base that sits on a table

r.x: The long-shank derivatives are rich enough to warrant their own entry; details are found in the Canadian family entry.
Prevalence and Cultural Standing

A striking example of the shape's central standing is the old numbering system used by Dunhill (White Spot) from the 1920s through the 1970s: according to records, this system alone had roughly fifty different codes just for Billiards. Among these, LB ("Large Billiard") came onto the market after the First World War and became one of the brand's most beloved shapes. The Bent Billiard, meanwhile, became something of a signature for Irish and English brands such as Peterson in particular; Peterson's System pipes are mostly produced with this body.

How widespread the shape is can also be seen by looking at manufacturers' shape numbers. According to records, Dunhill's 114, Comoy's 105, Peterson's 957, Savinelli's 1011, Stanwell's 03, Barling's 1100, and BBB's 606 all denote a straight Billiard; some manufacturers, such as Sasieni, have used place names like Pembroke or Buckingham instead of numbers. In the same lists, pot, chimney, bent, and army-mounted derivatives appear under separate numbers — meaning a single body family can fill dozens of lines in a catalog. It's also known that these numbering schemes changed across periods and that old brochures don't always agree with one another.

Because of its balanced bowl geometry, the Billiard is among the shapes most often recommended both to newcomers to pipe smoking and to those who want to get to know their tobacco blends: the bowl lets the tobacco speak for itself, without the shape getting in the way.

r.x: The long shanks

is a grouping name used to bring four classic shapes — Canadian, Lumberman, Liverpool, and Lovat — together under a single heading. All four preserve the Billiard body; what holds them together is that the shank is stretched well beyond the usual, with the mouthpiece (stem) shortened to compensate. The term doesn't come from any manufacturer's catalog — it was born from the community's own shape literature.
Source of the Term

The naming is credited to Bill Burney, author of the shape chart known as the ASP Pipe Shapes Chart, prepared within the alt.smokers.pipes newsgroup community. Burney describes the four shapes individually, but also states explicitly that the umbrella heading is his own coinage. What's at issue, then, isn't a historical production family distilled from catalogs, but a classification heading applied after the fact. Because the chart circulated freely online, it became one of the community's most consulted shape resources, and the group name spread along with it.
The Ratio That Defines the Group

The measure behind the distinction is simple. On a standard straight Billiard, shank length stays close to bowl height, while the mouthpiece is long. In the long shanks, this balance is reversed: the wooden section is stretched to at least one and a half times the bowl height, while the mouthpiece is shortened to balance the overall length. Lovat is considered the most measured member of the group; its shank most often stays near this lower limit, while its mouthpiece, like the other three, is kept long. How the four shapes diverge by shank cross-section (round or oval) and mouthpiece type (tapered or saddle) is detailed in the Canadian family entry.
Naming Confusion in Catalogs

The drift of shape names from one manufacturer to another shows up most in this group. In Dunhill catalogs, number 40 corresponds to Lovat and number 33 to Liverpool; according to shape lists, number 335 corresponds to Canadian, while the Lumberman name doesn't appear in these catalogs at all (Dunhill shape numbers). On the Charatan side, shapes numbered 0402 and 104, referred to as Lumberman, are known from estate pipe records; their official catalog counterparts haven't been confirmed, and their descriptions match the oval shank plus tapered mouthpiece combination — that is, the Canadian definition. In GBD listings, too, shape number 9465, matching the Lovat description, is reported to appear under the name Liverpool.

Amid this untidiness, Canadian and Lovat are considered the most solidly established names; Lumberman is regarded as the one with the fuzziest boundaries. In practice, some manufacturers continue to call all oval-shanked derivatives Canadian, others any long-shanked pipe at all. This is exactly where the umbrella heading earns its keep: when no consensus can be reached on an individual name, a pipe can at least be described with a shared definition.
The Cool-Smoke Debate

That a long shank gives a cooler, drier smoke is a view often voiced in the community; its basis is that smoke travels a longer wooden path before reaching the mouthpiece. This expectation has no measurement-based backing, and quite a few smokers say they don't notice the difference. A similar debate runs around churchwarden, with its far longer mouthpiece. The shape is therefore evaluated more as a matter of balance and appearance than of smoking performance.

r.x: Freehand

is an approach to shaping a pipe not according to a predetermined mold, but according to the grain structure of the briar block and the maker's design in the moment. It names a design philosophy more than a single shape with fixed dimensions: two freehands from the same workshop are never twins. The approach was born in Denmark in the mid-20th century and turned into a full-blown fashion wave in the United States market in the 1960s and 1970s. Today it's considered one of the founding traditions of handmade pipe making.
Distinguishing Features
The main elements that set the freehand approach apart from the classic pipe shapes in a catalog are:
Plateau edge:
The "plateau" — briar's naturally barked outer surface — is left as is, whether at the rim of the bowl or the end of the shank.
Following the grain:
The body follows the wood's grain direction; symmetry isn't sought, and the shape is built around what the block gives.
One-piece shank:
Long shanks are most often carved from the same block as the body.
Mixed surfaces:
Smooth and blasted or rusticated surfaces can be combined on the same pipe.
Birth and Rise

The technical foundation of the approach was laid in Copenhagen by Sixten Ivarsson: by reversing the traditional production order, he showed it was possible to shape the block first on the sanding disc and drill the bowl and airway afterward. This freedom opened the way for the first free-form shapes that broke away from classic molds. For the story of the broader design movement this approach grew out of, see the Danish School entry.

The person who popularized freehand in the US market, though, was Preben Holm (1947-1989). Holm, who started selling pipes to Copenhagen's well-known Pipe-Dan shop in 1963 at just sixteen, is reported to have been running a forty-five-employee workshop by the time he was twenty-two. According to records, after signing with the American company Lane Limited in 1971, Holm's hand-carved pipes were sold in the US under the "Ben Wade" brand, and they carried the "Danish fancy freehand" fashion to its peak, stunning a market accustomed to conservative English shapes. In the same period, makers such as Erik Nørding and Karl Erik Ottendahl brought well-crafted freehand pipes to a wide audience. Over time the movement developed along two branches: the flamboyant, swirling "fancy freehand," and the "Danish classic," seen as a fluid reinterpretation of classic shapes.
Freehand vs. Artisan

Freehand and artisan are often confused, but they aren't the same thing: freehand is an approach to shape, while artisan is a mode of production. Factories, too, have produced mass-market pipes with a freehand look; late-era Ben Wade production is a well-known example of this. For the details of the distinction, see the artisan pipe versus factory pipe entry.

And this is exactly where the movement's lasting legacy lies: the freehand wave turned the pipe from a mass-produced object into a signed design piece, laying the groundwork for the artisan generation that followed. The standards prized in today's high-end handmade pipes — grain integrity, single-block craftsmanship, preservation of natural texture — largely trace their roots back to this school.
